strengths: Introduces Moving Out, a physically-grounded human-AI collaboration benchmark that fills a genuine gap between discrete grid-world environments (OvercookedAI, Hanabi) and full simulators (Habitat 3.0), with continuous state-action spaces, physics-based interactions (shapes, sizes, mass, friction), and three distinct collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency).

Collected a substantial and carefully documented human dataset: 1,000+ human-human demonstrations from 36 participants (Task 1) and 720 expert demonstrations with randomized physical attributes (Task 2), with IRB approval, compensation details, and data collection procedures in the appendix.

Conducted both AI-AI and human-AI evaluations, including a human subject study with subjective Likert questionnaires and a failure-case analysis with quantified failure rate reductions (e.g., DP {0.797, 0.688, 0.906} to BASS {0.343, 0.563, 0.484}), which adds ecological validity beyond simulator scores.

Comprehensive appendices: environment comparison table, MAPPO reward design and hyperparameters, metric definitions, oracle-simulator upper-bound analysis, inference-speed discussion, and a cross-environment test of BASS on Overcooked AI showing ~15% improvement, partially supporting generality of the method.

Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges sparse-reward difficulties for RL, inference-speed constraints of generative models, incomplete coverage of physical interactions, and persistent failure modes.
weaknesses: Novelty of the benchmark relative to prior work is under-defended. The paper cites Du et al. [12] (Constrained Human-AI Cooperation, NeurIPS D&B) which is also a physically-grounded human-AI collaboration benchmark, but the differentiation from it and from Habitat 3.0 / HumanTHOR collaboration tasks is cursory; Table 2 compares only against Overcooked-AI and Table Carrying, omitting the most similar environment [12].

BASS is methodologically modest: partner-pose noise injection is standard data augmentation, the latent dynamics + one-step action scoring closely resembles existing world-model-scored planning (Wang et al. [25], Zhao et al. [29], which the authors themselves acknowledge), and the sub-trajectory recombination is a form of trajectory stitching whose validity is never actually verified (Sec. 5.1 admits validation is skipped, raising the risk of physically inconsistent training states).

Reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence: the main text states the human study had 32 participants and 'each participant played 32 maps', while Appendix I describes 12 volunteers and 12 maps with 50-second time limits; Table 1/Tables 6-7 contain typos ('BAAS', 'Diffuson', 'NDF'); the abstract's project-page URL is incomplete. These discrepancies make the user study hard to interpret.

Mixed and partially contradictory empirical evidence: several ablations show Full BASS is not best (e.g., GRU Task 2: w/o Augmentation 0.3670 vs Full BASS 0.3414 TCR; augmentation alone degrades MLP in both tasks); Table 6 shows DP has lower waiting time than Full BASS in Task 1 AI-AI (0.3075 vs 0.3448) while the text claims BASS reduces waiting time, without statistical significance testing on any quantitative results (only a t-test on Likert responses, p=0.017).

The core mechanism is weak where the paper claims it matters most: in Task 2 (generalization to unseen physical constraints), the next-state predictor agrees with the oracle simulator on only 48.7% of actions and leaves a large gap to the oracle bound (NFD 0.5535 vs 0.6209), suggesting limited physical understanding rather than genuine constraint reasoning.

Relevant baselines are missing: no comparison with zero-shot coordination / population-based methods (FCP, MAZE, HiPT, diverse conventions [33-36]) that are explicitly discussed in related work as state-of-the-art for adapting to diverse partners, leaving the claim that BASS 'outperforms state-of-the-art models' under-supported.

The action selection is a myopic one-step greedy argmax over a distance-to-goal heuristic, which the paper presents as enabling constraint-aware planning, but no analysis of rollout horizon, scoring function sensitivity, or compute trade-offs is provided.

strengths: The paper introduces a new physically grounded, continuous-space benchmark (Moving Out) for human-AI collaboration with three distinct collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency), addressing a genuine gap left by discrete environments like Overcooked-AI and Hanabi.

A substantial data collection effort: over 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 expert demonstrations for Task 2, with IRB approval and clear compensation details, which supports reproducibility and future model development.
A real human subject study (32 participants) evaluating collaboration with humans, including survey-based subjective feedback, which is more than many benchmark papers provide.

Ablations over BASS components (augmentation vs. simulation) and an oracle-simulator comparison (Appx. B) that quantifies the gap between the learned dynamics model and ground-truth physics simulation.
The limitations section is honest about inference-speed constraints and incomplete physical interaction coverage.
weaknesses: The central claim that BASS 'outperforms state-of-the-art models' is not well supported: the baselines are Bearer [REDACTED] cloning variants (MLP, GRU, Diffusion Policy) and MAPPO. The paper cites many modern zero-shot coordination methods (FCP, HSP, MAIC, population-based training, Liang et al. 2024) in Related Work but compares against none of them, so superiority over the actual state of the art is unverified.

The technical novelty of BASS is limited: Gaussian noise perturbation of partner poses, sub-trajectory recombination (closely related to existing trajectory stitching/data augmentation ideas), a small latent dynamics model, and greedy one-step action selection by reward argmax are each well-established components, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is new relative to prior world-model/action-selection work it cites (e.g., Wang et al., Zhao et al.).

Ablation results are mixed and sometimes contradict the narrative: in Task 2 with GRU, 'BASS w/o Augmentation' (TCR 0.3670) beats Full BASS (0.3414), and several improvements are within one standard error, yet the text claims full BASS 'achieves the highest overall performance in most cases' without statistical significance testing for the main results (a t-test is only reported for the subjective survey).

Internal inconsistency in the human study description: Section 6.1 states 32 participants evaluated BASS against DP, while Appendix I states the experiment was conducted with 12 volunteers, undermining confidence in the human evaluation.
The human-AI evaluation compares BASS only against the DP baseline, not against MLP, GRU, or MAPPO, so the claimed human-AI superiority over 'state-of-the-art' methods rests on a single comparison.

The MAPPO baseline requires author-designed dense, map-specific reward shaping (e.g., a special reward for Map 11's short sides), which raises concerns about the fairness and generality of the RL baseline and the resulting claim that the environment is challenging for RL.

The benchmark's scope is narrow: only 12 hand-designed 2D maps on top of the MAGICAL single-agent environment, and the connection to real embodied/robot collaboration claimed in the introduction is only motivational; no transfer or robotics experiments are shown.

Presentation and reproducibility gaps: the abstract's project-page URL is empty, and the paper contains several typos/editorial errors (e.g., 'play against an trained', 'Represented the save as walls'), suggesting insufficient polish. Key human-study quantitative results appear only in hard-to-read bar charts rather than tables.

strengths: The Moving Out benchmark fills a genuine gap: existing human-AI collaboration environments (Overcooked-AI, Hanabi, LBF) are discrete and lack physics, while Habitat 3.0/HumanTHOR are task- or navigation-level. The comparison table in Appx. A clearly positions the contribution.

Substantial empirical effort: over 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants (Task 1), 720 expert demonstrations with randomized physical attributes (Task 2), and a human subject study evaluating AI agents playing with humans — going beyond the AI-AI-only evaluations common in zero-shot coordination work.

BASS is evaluated with component-wise ablations on two backbones (GRU, Diffusion Policy), and Appx. B compares against an oracle simulator to quantify the gap of the learned dynamics model, which is a good practice for probing where the method loses performance.
Failure case analysis (Fig. 8, Appx. D) is honest and informative, explicitly quantifying how BASS reduces failure rates relative to DP and acknowledging remaining challenges.

Appropriate treatment of research ethics: IRB approval, participant compensation, and inference-speed constraints for real-time interaction are documented in the appendix; limitations (inference speed, incomplete physical coverage) are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the main text states a human study with 32 participants playing 32 maps, while Appx. I reports 12 volunteers; dataset counts shift between 1,000 demonstrations/2,000 action sequences (Sec. 1/4.3) and 720 demonstrations/1,440 action sequences. Statistical reporting is also thin — only a single t-test (p=0.017) is reported for subjective feedback, with no significance testing for the main quantitative comparisons in Fig. 6 or Table 1.

Some central claims are not supported by the presented numbers. The text claims ablation components 'improve task completion TCR and NFD compared to their base models,' yet in Table 1, MLP+BASS w/o Simulation (TCR 0.2952) is worse than MLP alone (0.3568) in Task 1, and Full BASS underperforms BASS w/o Augmentation for GRU in Task 2 (0.3414 vs. 0.3670). 'Highest overall performance in most cases' is an overstatement; component interactions appear inconsistent and unexplained.

The methodological novelty of BASS is modest: Gaussian pose perturbation, trajectory recombination, latent one-step dynamics models, and action scoring are all well-established (acknowledged in Sec. 2 via Wang et al., Yuan et al., Zhao et al., etc.). The recombination augmentation requires approximate state matching on a discretized 48x48 grid, and the paper admits generated trajectories may be physically invalid without validating them — the dynamics mismatch this introduces is not analyzed. The dynamics model is one-step only, so compounding error over the 8-action rollout horizon is unaddressed.

The claim that BASS 'outperforms state-of-the-art models' is weakly supported: baselines are vanilla BC (MLP, GRU), Diffusion Policy, and MAPPO with a bespoke dense reward. No zero-shot coordination / human-modeling methods from the cited literature (e.g., FCP, HSP, population-based approaches [15, 30-36]) are compared, which is the natural strongest baseline family for adapting to diverse partners.

The transfer claim that BASS generalizes beyond Moving Out rests on a single anecdotal Overcooked 'Cramped Room' result (15% improvement, no error bars or seeds reported), which is insufficient to support generality claims.

Presentation has notable defects: Section F.1.3 (Evaluation Setting) is empty, there are grammatical errors (e.g., 'play against an trained with diverse human behavior'), Figure 6 is too small to read axis labels, and the 'NDF/NFD' acronym is used inconsistently. These reduce readability and suggest the manuscript was not carefully finalized.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing human-AI collaboration benchmarks (Overcooked-AI, Hanabi, Watch-and-Help) use discrete/symbolic actions, while physically grounded, continuous-control collaboration has received far less attention. Moving Out fills this gap with a physics-based environment with diverse collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency).

The data collection effort is substantial and well-documented: over 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 demonstrations with randomized physical properties for Task 2, with IRB approval, participant compensation, and a documented diversity analysis (DTW, KDE entropy, coverage distance) supporting the claim that the dataset is more diverse than expert or RL-agent data.

The two evaluation tasks are thoughtfully designed with reproducibility in mind: the cross-group protocol (training on disjoint participant splits and evaluating AI-AI play) is a sensible proxy for generalization to unseen human behavior, and compositional randomization in Task 2 avoids memorization of physical attributes.

BASS is supported by thorough analysis: ablations of each component (Table 5), oracle-simulator upper bound (Table 4), next-state prediction accuracy comparisons (Table 9, 11), partner-action predictor analysis (Table 10), sampling-strategy study (Table 8), and an objective-selection comparison (Table 13).

A human subject study with real participants and a questionnaire provides direct evidence of human-AI collaboration quality (TCR 0.651 vs 0.386 for DP; significant survey differences), and the failure-case study (RQ4) is honest and informative about remaining limitations.
Comprehensive supplementary material (MAPPO hyperparameters, reward details, data collection procedures, map analyses) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Apparent numerical inconsistencies across tables undermine confidence in reported results: Table 2 reports DP seen-behavior TCR of 0.3233 and DP/BASS 0.3503, while the ablation tables (Table 5, 15) report DP 0.3829 and Full BASS 0.5027 for the same task and protocol. No explanation reconciles these discrepancies, which is a significant soundness/presentation concern.

The human study details are inconsistent: Section 6.1 states 32 participants, while Appendix R states 'In total, we conducted this experiment with 12 volunteers.' The statistical analysis of the questionnaire is thin (a single p-value for the pooled comparison), and the procedure in which volunteers select model IDs raises potential ordering/bias concerns that are not addressed.

Baseline comparison strength is limited. MAPPO is trained with a heavily engineered dense reward including map-specific modifications (e.g., Map 11 short-side grasping), which weakens it as a fair RL reference; more competitive recent zero-shot coordination approaches from the Overcooked literature are only touched via a single Cramped Room test (+15%), so the claim of outperforming 'state-of-the-art' is supported only within a small set of baselines.

Absolute performance remains low across all methods (TCR mostly 0.14-0.50 in AI-AI evaluation), suggesting the benchmark may be too difficult for current techniques to yield well-differentiated conclusions; differences between DP and DP/BASS in Table 2 are modest relative to reported standard errors, and significance tests for AI-AI results are not reported.

Methodological novelty of BASS is moderate: it is a combination of known components (diffusion policy backbone, latent dynamics/world model, trajectory stitching/augmentation), and the paper itself notes trajectory augmentation and stitching exist in single-agent settings [49, 50]; the multi-agent adaptation is a reasonable but incremental contribution.

The benchmark's scope is limited to 12 hand-designed maps in a 2D physics engine built on MAGICAL, and BASS's generalization beyond Moving Out is demonstrated on only one Overcooked map, so claims of broad applicability are under-evidenced.

Missing or broken project page link in the abstract (blank URL), and some typos/incomplete sentences (e.g., 'Represented the save as walls', 'the model select actions') suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Introduces a new physically grounded human-AI collaboration benchmark (Moving Out) with continuous state-action spaces and physics constraints, addressing a genuine gap relative to discrete benchmarks like Overcooked-AI, Hanabi, and LBF (Sec. 2, Table 3).

Substantial data collection effort: over 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 demonstrations from experts for Task 2, with IRB approval and quantified diversity analysis (DTW, KDE entropy, coverage; Table 1, Appx. B).

Comprehensive evaluation spanning AI-AI, AI-human collaboration, a human subject study (32 participants), failure case analysis, oracle-simulator comparisons, and extensive ablations of augmentation, dynamics model, sampling strategies, and partner prediction (Tables 4-16, Appx. C, K, L, M).

BASS is technically reasonable and well-motivated: multi-agent-aware trajectory augmentation with coherence guarantees (99% validity reported, Appx. H) plus learned latent dynamics for action selection, which is sensible when a simulator is unavailable at deployment.
The paper is honest about remaining limitations (failure modes persist, Fig. 9) and discusses the reproducibility motivation behind the cross-group proxy protocol (Appx. M).
weaknesses: The core evidence for 'adapting to unseen human behaviors' (Task 1) rests on a proxy protocol where two AI agents trained on disjoint human splits play each other (Sec. 4.2, Appx. M). Whether AI-AI cross-group play is a valid surrogate for adapting to real unseen humans is assumed rather than validated; the large AI-human gains (TCR 0.39 -> 0.65, Table 2) may reflect confounds (e.g., humans collaborating more with the stronger partner) and cannot be directly explained by the proxy.

Human study reporting is internally inconsistent: the main text claims 32 participants (Sec. 6.1) while Appx. R states 12 volunteers. Statistical support is thin — a single p-value (0.017) reported for the Likert survey without correction or effect sizes, and no significance testing on the headline human-AI collaboration metrics.

Absolute task performance remains low for all methods (best TCR ~0.35 in seen AI-AI settings), and the gap between proxy and human evaluation makes it unclear how much of BASS's advantage is benchmark-robust versus protocol-specific.

Baselines are relatively Bearer [REDACTED], GRU, vanilla diffusion policy, MAPPO with dense reward shaping described only in Appx. F). Notably, more relevant partner-modeling baselines from zero-shot coordination literature (e.g., population-based methods [24-28]) are cited but not empirically compared, despite direct relevance to adapting to unseen partners.

BASS is an assemblage of known ideas (trajectory stitching/augmentation [49, 50], model-predictive action selection with learned latent dynamics); the multi-agent coherence extension is a refinement rather than a fundamentally new methodological contribution.

Action selection uses hand-designed reward (NFD) with a bespoke grid/BFS distance; the justification for metric choices, and the sensitivity of results to them, receive only limited treatment (Appx. N shows NFD+AC degrades NFD).

Generalization in Task 2 is defined compositionally over a small set of shapes/sizes in 12 hand-crafted maps; the diversity claims would be stronger with procedural or larger-scale map variation, which the authors note is possible but do not demonstrate.

strengths: Introduces Moving Out, a physically grounded, continuous-control human-AI collaboration benchmark that addresses a genuine gap left by discrete/symbolic environments like Overcooked-AI, with a clear taxonomy of collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency) and 12 purpose-designed maps (Appx. U).

Substantial human data collection effort: ~1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants (Task 1) plus 720 expert demonstrations on randomized physical attributes (Task 2), with IRB approval, diversity quantification (Table 1, DTW/KDE/coverage metrics), and a reproduction-friendly cross-participant split protocol (Appx. M).

BASS is a sensible combination of behavior augmentation, a learned latent dynamics model, and action selection; the paper is unusually thorough in validation: ablations of each component (Table 5), comparison to an oracle simulator upper bound (Table 4), next-state prediction accuracy (Table 9), alternative dynamics models (Table 11), sampling-strategy analysis (Table 8), and a transfer test on Overcooked-AI.

A real human-subject study evaluates the model against a strong diffusion-policy baseline with both objective metrics and Likert-scale feedback, including failure-case analysis (RQ4) that is candid about remaining limitations.
Comprehensive supplementary material covering hyperparameters, reward design, data collection procedures, and full result tables supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency in the human study: Section 6.1 claims 32 participants while Appendix R states the experiment was conducted with only 12 volunteers; the abstract also ends with a missing project-page URL ('available at' with no link). These discrepancies undermine confidence in reported details.

The core 'adaptation to unseen human behaviors' claim (RQ1) is only indirectly evaluated: the cross-participant split protocol evaluates AI-AI cross-play between policies trained on disjoint groups, which is a proxy for, not a demonstration of, generalization to real unseen humans. The human study partially mitigates this but compares only DP vs. BASS with a small sample and a single reported p-value (p = 0.017) without correction for multiple questionnaire comparisons.

Absolute performance is low across the board (best TCR ~0.35 in AI-AI settings), and the DP/BASS gain over DP in the unseen-behavior protocol (0.301 vs. 0.256 TCR) is modest relative to the reported standard errors (Table 14), so the central robustness claim rests on a narrow margin; no significance testing is provided for the main tables.

The dataset-diversity comparison (Table 1) is somewhat circular: the 'expert dataset' and 'RL agent collected data' baselines were constructed by the authors, so the claim that recruiting diverse participants yields more diverse data is not established against any external reference point.

BASS's components (Gaussian pose perturbation, sub-trajectory stitching with boundary matching, greedy 1-step action selection with a learned world model) are individually well-trodden techniques; the novelty lies mainly in their careful adaptation to multi-agent physical collaboration rather than a fundamentally new method. Appx. T also shows BASS can hurt some backbones (e.g., MLP), suggesting the gains are backbone-dependent.

Task 2's evaluation via AI-AI self-play on unseen physical attributes does not test collaboration with humans under unseen physics, and self-play agents could co-adapt to each other's quirks in ways that overstate physical generalization.
The environment is a simplified 2D physics simulation; claims about relevance to embodied/robotic collaboration are plausible but not validated in any higher-fidelity setting.
